name: IT Band Syndrome
secondary_queries: IT band pain outside of knee
seo_title: IT Band Syndrome Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: IT band syndrome treatment in North Palm Beach for runners and cyclists. Hip strengthening, flexibility work and a graded return to running. 561-624-4263.
lede: IT band syndrome causes pain on the outside of the knee with running or cycling, and hip strengthening plus a graded return to activity is the usual first step.
what_it_is: Your iliotibial band is a thick strip of connective tissue that runs down the outside of your thigh from the hip to just below the knee, where it attaches to the shinbone. As the knee bends and straightens, the band moves over the outer edge of the thighbone. StatPearls notes the exact cause of pain is debated, with theories including friction against the bone, compression of a sensitive fat pad beneath the band and irritation of a small bursa.

According to StatPearls, IT band syndrome is the most common cause of outer knee pain in runners and cyclists, with reported rates of 1.6% to 12% among runners and other repetitive-motion athletes. Johns Hopkins Medicine notes it often affects distance runners and people new to exercise, especially with high mileage, worn shoes, uneven terrain or bowed legs. MedlinePlus adds poor conditioning and skipping a warm-up.
symptoms: Aching or burning pain on the outside of the knee
Pain that may spread up the outside of the thigh toward the hip
Mild pain when you start exercising that builds as you continue
Pain that is worse running downhill or climbing stairs
An ache after sitting a long time with the knee bent
Pain that starts earlier in exercise and lingers afterward as it progresses
causes: Repetitive knee bending in running and cycling
Sudden changes in mileage or activity level
Running on uneven surfaces or downhill
Skipping warm-ups or using poor technique

how_therapy_helps.intro: Conservative care is the standard first approach. StatPearls reports that physical therapy focused on stretching and hip abductor strengthening can be very effective, and that roughly 50% to 90% of patients improve with 4 to 8 weeks of non-operative care. MedlinePlus describes therapy that strengthens the core and hip muscles and stretches the surrounding tissue. Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that surgery is considered only after about six months of unsuccessful conservative treatment.
methods: Exercises for the muscles on the side of the hip, which help control how the thigh and knee move with each stride or pedal stroke.
Trunk and pelvic control work, since MedlinePlus lists core muscle imbalance as a contributing cause.
Stretching of the outer thigh and hip, plus foam rolling or myofascial release, which StatPearls describes as part of rehabilitation.

A look at running form, routes, shoes and training changes, along with sport-specific technique and posture, which StatPearls says the therapist should address during the activities that bring on the pain.
A stepwise plan that starts with flat-surface runs on alternating days and adds distance before hills, as outlined in StatPearls.

first_visit: Your therapist asks about your mileage, recent training changes, shoes and routes, then pinpoints where the pain sits on the outside of the knee. We test hip and core strength, check flexibility with the Ober test, and may use the Noble test, which presses on the outside of the knee as it straightens, to reproduce the pain. Watching a single-leg squat or step-down shows how your hip and knee move under load.
recovery: Most cases settle without surgery, though timing varies with how long you have had symptoms and how quickly training is adjusted. According to StatPearls, most patients have full symptom relief and return to activity within 6 to 8 weeks of non-operative management. A return-to-running progression typically spans several weeks, beginning on flat ground before hills and banked surfaces are added back. MedlinePlus advises building distance and speed slowly once stretching and strengthening are pain free.
self_care: Cut back on running or cycling, especially downhill running, until the pain settles
Ice the outside of the knee for 15 minutes every 2 to 3 hours, as MedlinePlus suggests
Use heat before exercise if it helps you warm up
Run on even surfaces rather than uneven or downhill terrain, as Johns Hopkins Medicine suggests
see_a_doctor: Pain that gets worse or does not improve in a few weeks (MedlinePlus)
The knee locks, gives way or is badly swollen (NHS)
You cannot put weight on the leg
Pain that started with a fall or direct blow to the knee
Fever with redness and warmth around the knee
Sharp pain directly over the bone with every step, since StatPearls lists stress fracture among conditions that can mimic ITBS

faqs.q: How long does IT band syndrome take to heal?
faqs.a: Many people improve within about two months. StatPearls reports that most patients have complete symptom relief and return to activity within 6 to 8 weeks of non-operative care, and that roughly 50% to 90% improve within 4 to 8 weeks. Recovery can take longer if symptoms have been present for a long time or training is not adjusted, and Johns Hopkins notes surgery is considered only after about six months.

faqs.q: Should I foam roll my IT band?
faqs.a: Foam rolling can be part of the plan. StatPearls describes myofascial release with a foam roller as part of IT band syndrome rehabilitation, alongside stretching and hip strengthening. It works best as one piece of a program rather than the whole treatment, because weak hip and core muscles and sudden training changes are common contributors that rolling alone does not address.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with IT band syndrome?
faqs.a: Usually you need to cut back first. StatPearls advises refraining from the activity that triggered the pain until it resolves, then returning gradually with flat-surface runs on alternate days, increasing distance after three to four weeks, and adding hills only when flat running is pain free. MedlinePlus similarly recommends slowly building distance and speed once exercises feel comfortable.

faqs.q: Why does IT band pain get worse running downhill?
faqs.a: Downhill running is a well-known aggravator. MedlinePlus notes that running down hills or sitting for a long time with the knee bent can make the pain worse, and StatPearls recommends avoiding downhill running early in the return-to-running plan. The repeated bending and straightening of the knee under load appears to irritate the tissue at the outside of the knee, so hills are usually added back last.

faqs.q: Could pain on the outside of my knee be something other than the IT band?
faqs.a: Yes. StatPearls lists several conditions that can cause similar outer knee pain, including a lateral meniscus tear, a lateral collateral ligament strain, arthritis in the outer part of the knee, hamstring tendon irritation, a stress fracture of the shinbone and pain referred from the hip. A therapist's evaluation can help tell these apart and flag when you should see a physician.

faqs.q: What exercises help IT band syndrome?
faqs.a: Hip abductor strengthening is central. StatPearls notes that physical therapy focused on hip abduction strengthening and IT band stretching can be very effective, and MedlinePlus describes strengthening the core and hip muscles. Side-lying leg raises, side planks, single-leg squats and step-downs are common examples, progressed over several weeks. Stretching the outer thigh and hamstrings is often added, as Johns Hopkins suggests.

signOrSymptom: pain on the outside of the knee
burning lateral knee pain while running
pain spreading up the outer thigh

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M76.3 (Iliotibial band syndrome) verified on icd10data.com; billable children M76.30/M76.31/M76.32.

Sources are moderate: StatPearls, MedlinePlus, Johns Hopkins and NHS. No ChoosePT or OrthoInfo ITBS page was available (ChoosePT URL returned 404), and no systematic review was fetched. StatPearls supplies all numeric claims (1.6% to 12% incidence; 50% to 90% improve in 4 to 8 weeks; most return within 6 to 8 weeks).
StatPearls was read at statpearls.com because the NCBI Bookshelf copy served a CAPTCHA; consider swapping the URL to https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542185/ if you prefer the NIH host.
Johns Hopkins lists corticosteroid injections as a treatment; not mentioned because the clinic does not offer them.
Example exercises named in the FAQ (side-lying leg raises, side planks, single-leg squats, step-downs) are standard hip abductor work but are not named verbatim in the sources; edit if preferred.

The downhill FAQ explanation ('repeated bending and straightening under load appears to irritate the tissue') is hedged inference consistent with StatPearls and Johns Hopkins rather than a direct quote.
